6.14.5.en: * Let us follow Him while He is persecuted and fleeing from the distress caused by His opponents, so that we too may [go up into a mountain and sit with Him](d). Thus we rise to a glorious grace, higher than everything, and reign with Him. As He Himself said: [Ye which have followed me in my trials, when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, in the regeneration, ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel] (Mt 19:28; Lk 22:28).

6.15.0.en: St. Cyril the Great Which are blackish by reason of the ice, and wherein the snow is hid [16].

6.15.1.en: They came in the appearance of a brook that offers water to the thirsty, yet they offered him water laden with mud, in which the ice is hid, and which cannot be drunk.

6.15.2.en: Job groans because of the muddy consolations of his friends, which are full of mire. For out of the dregs of their earthly hearts they offer mire, and out of the coldness of their love they offer snow. So it is with every soul that places its hope in the consolations of men: it receives nothing but mire and ice, which, instead of refreshing wounded souls, crush them by the earthly, temporal thinking and the spiritual coldness that they conceal.

6.15.3.en: But whoever receives the consolations of the Holy Spirit, which lift the soul up to heaven, free it from the mire of this world, and grant it the warmth of the Spirit, has his earthly heart changed by the water of the Spirit into a heavenly paradise. The Spirit removes from within him every love of earthly things, so that he sings, "[He] hath made us sit together in heavenly places." He scatters every coldness of the soul, bestowing a surpassing flame of love that all the waters of the world cannot quench.

6.15.4.en: * He (the Holy Spirit) is called the Comforter, because He comforts and gladdens those who are in tribulations.

6.15.5.en: St. Macarius the Great * The Holy Spirit whom He would send was called the Comforter, given this title because of His work. For He not only gives rest to those whom He finds worthy and delivers them from every grief and disturbance in the soul, but at the same time grants them a sure joy that never dissolves. An eternal joy dwells in their hearts, where the Holy Spirit dwells.

6.15.6.en: * It is impossible for anyone to receive the grace of God unless he has the Holy Spirit, in whom are all the gifts of God.

6.15.7.en: St. Didymus the Blind * When the soul is filled with the fruit of the Spirit, it is stripped entirely of gloom, distress and weariness, and puts on spaciousness, peace and joy in God, and opens in its heart the door of love for all people.

6.15.8.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * The kingdom of the pure soul is within his heart; the sun that shines in it is the light of the Holy Trinity; the air of its breeze is the Holy Spirit the Comforter; those who dwell there with him are the natures of the pure spiritual beings; and their life, joy and delight is Christ, the radiance of the Father...

6.15.9.en: * Whoever looks within himself to our Lord, and whose soul is mingled with His light, has his heart filled with joy.

6.16.0.en: The Spiritual Elder What time they wax warm, they vanish: when it is hot, they are consumed out of their place [17].

6.16.1.en: Job likens his friends to a brook that has become dry because of the heat, with not a drop of water in it to drink. Travelers turn aside to it, hoping to quench their thirst and the thirst of their animals; they leave the road of their journey and go to it over great distances, almost losing their way, only to be surprised by its dryness, and so shame comes upon them.

6.16.2.en: It did not stop at there being mud in the waters of the brook; rather, it quickly dries up, and Job goes to it to drink, and finds a dry streambed.

6.16.3.en: What is meant by the word "wax warm"? Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that those on whom chastisements fall have their minds become hot, inflamed with the fires of fruitless remorse, because they do not think of eternal things but are occupied with temporal glory. Their remorse therefore crushes them all the more, and they melt away in their place.

6.16.4.en: * [You who are terrified before me, behold, they have cast me down like ice or thick snow, which, when it melts at the approach of the heat, can no longer be distinguished](e). He says: It is as though sorrows have pressed upon me from every side, and those subject to me and my companions have become against me. Not only has the law of love been annulled, but even the awe that leads to obedience has vanished. As for me, who wrestle with trials and violent passions, I have become like frozen snow, which, when the season of heat comes, dissolves and vanishes and no trace of it remains. It leaves no signs behind it, because the king, who is I, sits on a dunghill. The one who wore purple has become utterly naked outside the city. He sits outside to spend the night, he who formerly dwelt in splendid dwellings, whose houses were overlaid with gold and silver in abundance. He who was surrounded by many servants is now forsaken. He who had many sons and inherited crowns has suddenly come to ruin; he has lost all the wealth of his house.

6.16.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * This garment that you put on within Baptism, O man, has light for its warp and Spirit for its weft, and it is flame. The Father prepared it for you, the Son wove it for you, and the Spirit fashioned it for you. You went down into the waters and put it on divinely. The Trinity gave fire in Baptism to burn up iniquity and that souls may live with God.

6.17.0.en: St. Jacob of Sarug The paths of their way are turned aside (the caravans turn aside from their way); they go to nothing, and perish (they enter the wilderness and perish) [18].

6.17.1.en: The brook turned away from those in need of it, so that the thirsty find no water to drink. So the friends, with their consolations, moved far away from Job, and became like a stream of water that flees from the thirsty. But the Holy Spirit the Comforter waters the soul and satisfies it, so that it needs nothing.

6.17.2.en: * It is known, my brethren, that each of us seeks his rest and his joy, but he does not seek it as he ought, nor where it is to be found. Everything depends on distinguishing true joy from false joy; on the contrary, we are often deceived by the phantoms of vain joy and false good.

6.17.3.en: The miser, the arrogant, the glutton and the lustful each seeks joy, but one places his joy in amassing great wealth, another in the honor of ranks and dignities, another in delicious food and drink, and another in satisfying his unclean desires. None of them seeks his joy as he ought, nor where it is to be found; therefore none of them finds it, though all of them desire it.

6.17.4.en: Everything in the world cannot satisfy the soul and give it true joy. Why then do you weary yourself, foolish man, wandering in vain through many places, expecting to find good things with which to fill your soul and please your body?! Love one good that contains all goods, for in it alone you will find sufficiency.

6.17.5.en: Rest in the one great and universal Good, for in Him is sufficiency for everything.

6.17.6.en: And you, O my soul, bless the Lord, who satisfieth thy mouth with good things (Ps 103:2, 5).

6.17.7.en: St. Augustine The troops of Tema looked.

6.18.0.en: The companies of Sheba waited for them (the processions of Sheba waited for them) [19].

6.18.1.en: The caravans of Tema and Sheba, the caravans of the merchants of those lands in the Arabian desert, looked to the waters and hoped to drink from them, but they were ashamed when the waters fled from them.

6.18.2.en: The blessed Job asks us to consider the paths of Tema and the ways of Sheba. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Tema is translated "south wind" and Sheba is translated "net." So the man who is not occupied with eternal things is like one upon whom the hot south wind blows, making his life dissolute as by the working of heat, and his feet become like those caught in a net or bound with the fetters of temporal things.

6.18.3.en: They were ashamed in that wherein they were confident.

6.19.0.en: They came thither, and were ashamed [20].

6.19.1.en: When travelers in the wilderness head toward a well-known brook, they feel relieved because they are confident that they will find water to drink; but their confidence is utterly shattered when they find it dry. Such is Job's position toward his friends, in whom he thought he would find his consolations, only to find that they offer dry words and hearts without love, so that his hope in them is utterly disappointed.

6.19.2.en: His confidence was great that he would drink from the waters of the brook in the midst of the wilderness. But his assurance proved vain.

6.19.3.en: The friends came to Job and were ashamed, and as Pope Gregory (the Great) says, they were unable to shake the saint's mind with their harsh, bitter criticism.

6.19.4.en: These are the feelings of the blessed Job, that his friends have been put to shame, since with all their slanders they failed to bring him into despair, but they themselves became confused through the madness of their violent folly.

6.19.5.en: * [They are ashamed while I hope.] When the wicked direct their evils at the righteous, and see their inward hope shaken, they rejoice, because their deceit has borne fruit. They count the spreading of their errors the greatest gain they have acquired, rejoicing when their fellows perish. But when the hope of the righteous man is rooted within and is not shaken nor bowed to the earth by outward evils, the souls of the wicked are put to shame because they are unable to reach the depths of those in trial, and they are abashed, since their violence appears to have no purpose.

6.19.7.en: In the opinion of Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem, Job says to them: "Look at your provinces subject to tribute, or at your neighbors, as at your roads. For you surely realize that, though they thought themselves more renowned than others, they are yet worthy of blame." Shame covers those who trust in their cities and their wealth, which Job had in abundance. When he was struck by trials, God removed all this from him; therefore their confidence in what is theirs is mistaken, and soon their pride will be annulled and their haughtiness will perish.

6.19.8.en: For now ye are like them.

6.20.0.en: Ye see my casting down, and are afraid [21].

6.20.1.en: Job assures his friends that they have become like this deceptive brook, which waters no one and gives no consolation, but offers mirage and deceit... Such are the vain consolations of men; they are nothing at all!

6.20.2.en: "Ye see my casting down, and are afraid." It is as though he says: When I was in prosperity you flattered me, at a time when I did not need your flattery. And when the blow fell on me, you were afraid, and gave me bitterness instead of sweet words, and sharp criticism instead of consolations.

6.20.3.en: * [Now you have come and seen my blow, and you are afraid]... It is as though he says plainly: "I feared God when I was supported by prosperity and did not feel the wounds of the blow. But you did not fear God out of love; you were terrified of Him only through the blows of the rod.

6.21.0.en: Did I say, Bring unto me? or, Give a reward for me of your substance? [22]

6.21.1.en: Even though he had been reduced to a state of nothingness, he asked nothing from them, did not burden them in anything, did not ask for money, and did not put them to any expense. Why then do they take this painful attitude?

6.22.0.en: Or, Deliver me from the enemy's hand? or, Redeem me from the hand of the mighty? [23]

6.22.1.en: He did not ask them to rescue him from an enemy or from the hand of the mighty, nor did he ask them to pay a ransom to deliver him. Thus Job was chaste in soul, even when he reached the bitterest condition of poverty.

6.23.0.en: Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred [24].

6.23.1.en: Job differed with them in opinion, yet he was not stubborn, but was ready to accept the truth if he was in error, saying, "Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred."

6.23.2.en: In the midst of affliction, when someone rebukes us, especially if he is prejudiced against us, it is hard to listen to him or accept his counsel, as we fix our eyes on his evil prejudice and his exploitation of our distress to crush us. But Job, in the midst of affliction, declares to his friends that he is ready to listen and hear, and that if they point out a fault in his life he will correct himself.

6.23.3.en: What a wonderful picture of a soul that, though troubled by the bitterness of successive calamities, carries inner calm and a marvelous readiness to accept the counsel of his friends, whatever their intentions.

6.23.4.en: * "Teach me." Behold, you see Job listening to you in silence. In my sorrows, am I rebellious? Do I not feel the flood of the trial? I am not closed to accepting counsel. If you refute me because I am mistaken, you will see me hasten to correct the situation.

6.23.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * This means: I asked nothing of you in the past, nor have I asked anything of you now, and you have come on your own initiative to find me and comfort me. Why then do you treat me as an enemy? [Teach me, and I will hold my tongue; if I am erring in anything, tell me.]

6.23.6.en: In any case, even under these circumstances I do not refuse to learn, as long as you speak what is profitable. And I will keep silent if you utter acceptable words.

6.23.7.en: Surely they cannot present clear accusations, but only guesses and conjectures.

6.23.8.en: Since a person's life was clearly full of virtues, it was fitting for them not to see in the chastisements what they say.

6.23.9.en: St. John Chrysostom God alone is absolutely perfect; He teaches the whole world and has no need to be taught. But we, as shepherds who serve by God who dwells in us, must always have an expanding heart, continuing to expand in order to receive from God, so that the fragrance of Christ may spread the more in us, for however great the expansion of our heart, it is only a tiny point in comparison with the depth of God's love and His infinite abundance.

6.23.10.en: A shepherd, even if he is a patriarch, if he is not always learning, his growth stops, his stagnation shows, and he stumbles his people in their spiritual growth. But to the extent that he bows low at the feet of the Lord, opens his heart to Him in prayer and in the study of the Holy Bible, and always listens with all his heart to learn the judgments of God in every matter, he grows in his fellowship with Him, and his flock grows with him as well.

6.23.11.en: * I cannot escape the work of teaching, since the priesthood has been laid upon my shoulders, though I tried to flee from it(f).

6.23.12.en: And I desire to strive in learning so that I may be able to teach.

6.23.13.en: For there is one Master (God) who alone does not learn what He teaches to all.

6.23.14.en: But men must learn before they teach, and receive from God their Teacher what they teach others.

6.23.15.en: St. Ambrose * Read the Holy Scriptures continually, and never lift the Holy Bible from your hand. Learn what you will teach others, holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that you may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers (1 Tim 3:4), "But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them." [Be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you] (1 Pet 3:15).

6.24.0.en: St. Jerome How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove? [25]

6.24.1.en: Job was not at ease with their manner of dealing with the matter; it was fitting for them to converse with him in a spirit of love and uprightness. But to use the method of criticism and rebuke based on groundless assumptions and conjectures is not for edification.

6.24.2.en: * [Well! The words of a true man seem to be worthless.] He says: It seems to me that I am unable to lead the battle, because my adversaries oppose me, and because when the truth is spoken and openly declared, there is no one to listen to it. For the words of the righteous man seem worthless to everyone.

6.24.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * [Since the words of a true man seem vain.] They are vain for those who are not truly so. But when I look at you, I do not know whom you are serving?!

6.25.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind? [26]

6.25.1.en: Rebuking in a spirit of violence and with harshness will not bear fruit.

6.25.2.en: * [I ask of you neither a word nor strength, nor does your rebuke make me cease from speaking.] Yes, for even if it were fitting for you to judge my case according to the present circumstances, I do not entreat you... [for I do not seek strength from you]... I pay no heed to the sounds of this speech of yours, besides that you attack the fatherless and wrong one of your friends. He tells them that neither enmity nor friendship has any effect on you. In any case, if you wish, let me return to my saying: [I ask nothing.] For even if you take a stand of opposition, I repeat once more: my conscience does not rise up against me.

6.26.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Yea, ye overwhelm the fatherless, and ye dig a pit for your friend! [27]

6.26.1.en: As Job looks at their conduct toward the fatherless as toward their friends, he can repeat: [My conscience will not rebuke me by your words.]

6.26.2.en: He likens them, as they rebuke him while he is in a bitter state and in calamity, to one who humiliates an orphan unable to repel insults.

6.26.3.en: Job counted himself, having lost his children, like an orphan who has lost his parents, needing their tenderness so that they might be like God, since He is "a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows" (Ps 68:5).

6.26.4.en: What grieves him is that they, being his friends, set a trap into which he falls, instead of supporting him to come out of the trap of successive trials.

6.26.5.en: * [Yes, you crush and exert yourselves to destroy me.] He shows how weak he is, for he calls himself [an orphan]. When love is wounded, it does not take away love; therefore he immediately complains that they are destroying him, and yet testifies that he is their friend.

6.26.7.en: * Every monk (man) who seeks perfection and desires to strive lawfully in his spiritual combat must rid himself entirely of the sin of anger and wrath, and heed the warning addressed to him by the "chosen vessel," who says: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice" (Eph 31:4). And when he says: [Let all anger be put away from you], he excepts no one, whatever the necessity or what is profitable for us; and if need arises, any erring brother must be treated at once in a manner that will not make him like a person who went to treat a patient with a slight fever and entangled himself in his own anger and wrath, so that he lost his sight and insight. For he who wishes to heal another's wound must himself be sound and whole, suffering from no weakness, lest the saying of the Gospel be addressed to him: "Physician, heal thyself" (Lk 4:23), and lest, while he sees the mote that is in his brother's eye, he does not see the beam that is in his own eye. For how can he see well enough to cast the mote out of his brother's eye, he who has in his own eye the beam of anger? (Mt 7:3-5)

6.27.0.en: St. John Cassian Now therefore be content, look upon me; for it is evident unto you if I lie [28].

6.27.1.en: Job was truthful with himself as with others; therefore he asked them to look closely at him and reconsider the matter, for he does not lie nor deceive anyone.

6.27.2.en: It is as though he says to them: Do not hunt for some of my words; look at my face, for even though I cursed the day of my conception and the day of my birth, which is what you are hunting for, I did not blaspheme my God.

6.27.3.en: Look closely at my sores, for they are unbearable, and what my tongue utters is not without reason. I am not contending with my God.

6.27.4.en: Return, I pray you, let it not be iniquity.

6.28.0.en: Yea, return again, my righteousness is in it [29].

6.28.1.en: He returns and repeats, calling on them to think again; he asks them to return to themselves and not to be prejudiced against him, that they may see his right. For if he was not able to keep his calm, this does not mean that he lost his uprightness and nobility.

6.29.0.en: Is there iniquity in my tongue? cannot my taste discern perverse things? [30]

6.29.1.en: He asks them whether he uttered with his tongue any word of blasphemy against God. What iniquity do they accuse him of? Is not what he uttered commensurate with the bitterness he suffers?

6.29.2.en: * When we expose our brother's sin, God exposes our sin, and when we tell people of our brother's crime, God does the same with us.

6.29.3.en: One of the Desert Fathers * Guard your tongues, by not speaking evil of your brethren. For he who speaks evil of his brother angers God who dwells in him. What each one does to his companion, he does to God.

6.29.5.en: Aim the arrows of Your love at my heart

6.29.6.en: * In the midst of the distress of this world my soul groans within me!

6.29.7.en: Does anyone perceive the weight of my cross?

6.29.8.en: Does anyone share the bitterness of my soul!

6.29.9.en: My troubles have flooded over my head, and my heart is greatly distressed.

6.29.10.en: * My Lord, expose my sin before my eyes; instead of crying out from the multitude of afflictions, let me sink into the depth of Your love, O Forgiver of sins and Deliverer of my soul from corruption!

6.29.11.en: I no longer see in my heart the enemy's arrows, aflame with fire.

6.29.12.en: Rather, in the midst of distress I see the arrows of Your love piercing my depths.

6.29.13.en: My whole being turns into a joyful wedding.

6.29.14.en: I sing and chant: I am wounded with love!

6.29.15.en: * I no longer look for comfort from men, nor do I feel any longer the triviality of my life!

6.29.16.en: Though my life has become like loathsome food without salt, by Your love I see You as the true salt who pours sweetness upon my depths.

6.29.17.en: In You I become the salt of the earth and the light of the world!

6.29.18.en: I no longer lament my weakness, for You are my strength and my help.

6.29.19.en: * In the midst of my distress the consolations of men have become a burden on my soul.

6.29.20.en: From their channels they offer muddy waters that hide ice within them.

6.29.21.en: But You, O heavenly Comforter, give me Your Spirit within me as a spring of living water, refreshing my soul and renewing my life; You remove all dust within me, and turn my desert into a heavenly garden.

6.29.22.en: There is no place for ice within me, for Your Spirit is a blazing flame of fire; who can quench it?

6.29.23.en: * My friends criticize me in order to justify themselves; they display their human wisdom without sincere love.

6.29.24.en: But You are the wonderful Teacher, You teach by the commandment full of love.

6.29.25.en: You speak with me that I may speak with You; You guide me and carry me in Yourself, and lift me up to the bosom of Your Father, justified in You!

6.29.26.en: * The rebukes of men often drive me to despair and crush my depths, so that I long for death.

6.29.27.en: Your rebukes carry a tender fatherhood: they wound and bind up, they uproot the tares from Your field, that You may plant Your paradise in my depths; Your firmness carries surpassing sweetness.

6.29.28.en: Your glances carry with the rebuke a surpassing tenderness!

6.29.29.en: * Be You my unique Friend; Your words are serious, full of sweetness!

6.29.30.en: Your glances grant hope, and crush my soul with love!

6.29.31.en: Meeting with You turns my heart into a temple for You.

6.29.32.en: Your touches set my whole being aflame that I may run to You!

6.29.33.en: Come and dwell in me, and I will dwell in You forever.
